title: The Nations Scattered from Here — Names, Lands, Peoples
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Here is a chapter most people turn straight past when they read: Genesis 10, a list of seventy nations. Page after page of names, and most of them you do not recognise and cannot even pronounce.
I want to ask you not to skip it. Because this chapter is in fact the world map of the whole Bible — and it is saying something quite extraordinary.

The question this lesson asks is a very ordinary one: have you ever met someone in church who is unlike you in every single way, someone you find hard to get along with? A different temperament, a different way of getting things done, even a different way of praying. And every time we meet a person like that, the same thought comes up inside us: why can't he be a bit more normal?

Let me put the answer up front: diversity is not the curse of Babel; diversity is what God made. And what finally makes the seventy nations one is the grace that narrows the camera down onto a single man.
1. A Genealogy That Does Not Look Like a Genealogy

Verse 1: "Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." This is the fourth "generations" in the book, תּוֹלְדֹת (*toledot*). Every time that word appears, the camera has to change.

Brothers and sisters, if you are going to grasp how unusual this chapter is, you first have to know what genealogies were for in the ancient world. In that age every empire wrote genealogies for the same purpose: to prove "I am nobler than you." The king of Egypt said he was the son of the sun god; the king of Babylon said his bloodline came down from the gods. A genealogy was a political document, and its function was to put people in rank order.

Then look at Genesis 10: Shem, Ham and Japheth, three branches, written down side by side and on the level. Not one nation is fathered by a god. Not one nation is born to slavery. There is not a single sentence anywhere saying "this branch is the nobler one." All of them are the sons of Noah; all of them came out of the same family after the flood.

Brothers and sisters, in the ancient world this was a revolutionary document. In Acts 17:26 Paul stands in Athens and says, "He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth." This chapter is what he is talking about.

And you will notice that a great many of the "names" on this list are in fact place names or the names of peoples. "Mizraim", מִצְרַיִם (*Mitsrayim*), is Egypt — and the Hebrew word for Egypt is a dual form, because in that period Egypt was divided into an upper and a lower half. "Canaan", כְּנָעַן (*Kena'an*), is the very land Israel would later go in to take. So this is a genealogy and a map of the ancient world at the same time.
A genealogy like the one in chapter 10 — is it all right to skip it when you are reading the Bible?

You can skip it, but you will miss two things. First, this is the only list in the whole Bible that gathers every nation of the then-known world into one place, and every one of them comes from the same father — right at the very beginning the Bible cuts off any possibility that one people might be innately higher than another. Second, this list is a funnel: the seventy names are set out, then the camera closes onto the line of Shem, and then onto one man, Abraham. So it is not a heap of data; it is a camera movement in the storytelling. A practical suggestion for reading it: you do not have to memorise the names, but do watch two things — where each branch goes, and who the text stops for in order to write a few extra sentences. Wherever it stops, that is the point.
Does the number seventy carry a special meaning?

The traditional count of the nations in chapter 10 comes to seventy, and seventy turns up again several times later in Scripture: Jacob's whole household goes down to Egypt as seventy persons (Genesis 46:27); Moses appoints seventy elders (Numbers 11:16); the Lord Jesus sends out another seventy (Luke 10:1). It is hard to call those echoes coincidence, and Jewish tradition has always tied "seventy" to "all the nations." But be careful not to turn it into numerology. The safe way to put it is this: in Scripture seventy carries the flavour of complete representation, so what this list is saying is — here is the whole human race, and nobody has been left out. And God's promise to Abraham, "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you", is pointing at exactly these seventy nations.
2. A Light from the Original: "Everyone After His Language" Is Written Before Babel
Now I want you to look at a detail that matters enormously — a detail that will settle how you understand this whole business of people being different.
Verse 5: "Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in their nations." Verses 20 and 31 repeat exactly the same formula.
"Everyone after his language" is אִישׁ לִלְשֹׁנוֹ (*ish lilshono*), literally "each man according to his own tongue."
Brothers and sisters, turn over to the next chapter. Genesis 11:1 says, "The whole earth was of one language and of one speech." Only then comes Babel, and only then does God confuse their speech.

Do you see the problem? Chapter 10 says the languages have already divided; chapter 11 says the language was one to begin with. This is not a contradiction — it is Moses arranging his material on purpose. He shows you the outcome first — seventy nations, each with its own tongue — and only then rewinds to tell you the cause.

And the intention behind that arrangement matters a great deal: the author wants you to see diversity first as a normal, blessed picture, and only after that to read Babel. So the multiplicity of languages is not in itself a curse. What comes under judgement is the Babel kind of unity — the unity that says, "let's make a name for ourselves."

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously for the church. The opposite of unity is not difference; the opposite of unity is division. God has never wanted to turn everybody into the same thing. 1 Corinthians 12 says the body has many members and they are not alike, and Paul asks, "If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?"

And then there is that word in verse 32: "divided", נִפְרְדוּ (*nifredu*), a passive form. They did not scatter themselves; they were divided. The scattering is something God did. And Acts 17:26 goes straight on to say that God had "determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings." Even where they scattered to was inside his plan.
"Everyone after his language, after their families, in their nations" is written before the tower of Babel. Has the order gone wrong?

Nothing has gone wrong. This is a way of writing that the Bible uses often: give the result first, then go back and account for the cause. Chapter 10 is the aerial view — the nations have already been scattered. Chapter 11 is the close-up — why they were scattered. The same technique turns up more than once in Genesis. And it is very useful for our own Bible reading: do not assume the text has made a mistake the moment the chronology looks out of order; ask first, "why has the author arranged it this way?" Here the arrangement carries a theological point. He lets you see first that the scattering of the nations is God's own intention — the "fill the earth" of chapter 1 — and only then lets you see the one occasion when human beings resisted that scattering and failed. Arranged like this, Babel is not merely a judgement; it is also God bringing people back to the commission they were given in the first place.
3. Nimrod: the One Man in the Chapter with a Story
In a list that is almost nothing but names, there is one man for whom the text comes to a halt and spends five whole verses.

Verses 8 to 10: "Cush became the father of Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before Yahweh. Therefore it is said, 'like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before Yahweh'. The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar."

The word behind "a mighty one" is גִּבֹּר (*gibor*) — a warrior, a man of power. Brothers and sisters, where did we last meet that word? Genesis 6:4: "The Nephilim were in the earth in those days … Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown." The same word. The author is drawing a line.
And the word behind "men of renown" — "name", שֵׁם (*shem*) — is one of the words this whole book keeps tracking. In a moment you will meet it again in 11:4: "let's make a name for ourselves."

So who is Nimrod? The text passes its verdict on him in a very restrained way: it does not scold him outright, it simply writes down the names of his cities — "The beginning of his kingdom was Babel." Brothers and sisters, the reader will work it out for himself. The builder of the first empire; his first city called Babel; and in the very next chapter Babel goes wrong.

The sentence "He was a mighty hunter before Yahweh" has been read in different ways down the centuries. Some read it as straight praise: "before Yahweh" would mean an excellence that everybody acknowledged. Others read it the other way, because in the inscriptions of the ancient Near East "hunter" is very often how a conqueror described himself — and what he hunted was not wild animals but people. These notes lean towards the second reading, and the reason is that city name.

And I want to ask a question that comes closer to home: what is the difference between a hunter and a shepherd? A hunter counts how much he has taken; a shepherd counts how well the sheep are doing. Both of them spend their lives with animals — one brings back a carcass, the other brings back a flock. And the Lord Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep."
Nimrod is called "a mighty hunter". Is the text praising him?

The text passes no direct comment, and that is part of what makes it so intriguing. But there are several clues we can be sure of. He is the only man in the chapter with a story. The word "mighty" (גִּבֹּר) is the same word used in chapter 6 for the "mighty men" before the flood. The kingdom he founded had its beginning at Babel — precisely the city of the tower in the next chapter. And out of his territory came Assyria and Nineveh, the two great empires that oppressed Israel in the Old Testament. So most interpreters hear a reserved, even a negative, note in it. The practical reminder this passage gives us is this: a person's ability, his achievements and his reputation can be written down in Scripture without that amounting to approval. What you have to look at is where he took those abilities.
Does the phrase "before Yahweh" mean that Nimrod feared God?

The Hebrew לִפְנֵי יְהוָה is literally "before Yahweh", and it can be a neutral "in God's sight"; some interpreters read it with a note of defiance, "right in Yahweh's face." Both readings have their defenders, and the text itself does not settle the question. What these notes do is set both of them out, and then take hold of one thing that is certain: whichever way you read it, the phrase reminds us that everything a human being does happens in God's presence. That is of more use to us than the argument is — what you did today, what you said, the message you pressed send on, all of it was done "before Yahweh." The phrase is itself a way of living.
From verse 21 the text turns to the descendants of Shem, and there are several very interesting things in this section.

First, although Shem is the eldest, he is dealt with last. This is Genesis's standard technique: finish off the side branches, then come back to the main line. Ishmael's descendants are set out before Isaac's; Esau's descendants are set out before Jacob's. It is the same way of writing every time.
Second, verse 21 calls Shem "the father of all the children of Eber." "Eber" is where the name "Hebrew" would later come from. The author has quietly set down a signpost here.

Third, verse 25 says, "To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided." Peleg means "division". The text has hidden the memory of that scattering inside a name.

Brothers and sisters, if you follow the line of Shem downward, you will find the list getting narrower and narrower. From seventy nations it closes onto the line of Shem; from the line of Shem onto Eber; from Eber onto Peleg; and from 11:10 the counting carries on down until it comes to rest on one man — Terah's son, Abram.

This is the camera language of Genesis: first it shows you the whole world, seventy nations; then it narrows, and narrows, and narrows, until at last it rests on an old man who has no son. And in the first promise God speaks to that old man, the last sentence is this: "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you."

Brothers and sisters, do you see the structure? The seventy nations of chapter 10 are precisely the roll-call behind "all the families" in chapter 12. God narrows in order to scatter wide again. He chooses one in order to bless them all.
If all the nations share one origin, why does racism still exist? How should Christians respond?

From beginning to end chapter 10 is saying one thing: every nation came out of the same household. Acts 17:26 puts it even more plainly: "He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth." So within the Bible's view of the world, racial superiority has not a single leg to stand on. The reason discrimination is still with us is that the human heart, from chapter 3 onwards, uses difference to rank people so that it can stand a little higher itself. The Christian response has three layers. First, dismantle that measuring stick inside your own heart. Second, in your speech, take no part in any joke made at the expense of an ethnic group. Third, in what you actually do, deliberately welcome the person who is "not like us." Chapter 10 lists seventy nations, and God did not leave a single one of them out.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching many languages and many peoples as the curse of Babel. We have already seen it: chapter 10's "everyone after his language" is written before the confusing of speech in chapter 11, and Moses arranged it that way on purpose. If you preach difference as a problem that needs correcting, your congregation will start dealing with everyone unlike themselves by way of assimilation. And that is the spirit of Babel, not the Spirit of God.

The second is using the table of nations to argue that some modern people is superior or inferior. The purpose of this list is exactly the opposite: it writes every nation down side by side as equals. There have been people in history who took the genealogies of the Bible and used them to prop up doctrines of racial superiority, to justify colonisation and slavery. That is a betrayal of the text. Here is the test: when you have finished preaching, is there any chance your congregation could take this chapter away and think less of any group of people?

The third is preaching Nimrod as a straightforward hero story. Some people handle this passage by putting the weight on "look how capable he was, how bold, he built an empire out of nothing" — and it turns into a success seminar. Verse 10 says "the beginning of his kingdom was Babel"; the text ties him to Babel deliberately. Preach the ability and never the direction, and what the congregation learns is ambition, not reverence.

The fourth is treating this chapter as mere data and hurrying past it. I know it is a hard chapter to preach, because it is nothing but names. But if you dispose of it in two minutes, what your congregation learns is that "there are parts of the Bible you are allowed to skip." And this chapter is in fact the root of mission: every family on the face of the earth is on God's register.

The fifth is forcing every ancient people onto some country on today's map. Some of the identifications are quite clear — Mizraim is Egypt, Canaan is the land of Canaan — but other names are still disputed among scholars. Preaching a guess as a settled conclusion weakens your credibility everywhere else. Saying honestly, "this one we are not sure about", will actually make a congregation trust you more.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese people set great store by coming from the same district, the same clan, by being "one of us", and churches too very often divide naturally into a few circles — those who speak the same dialect, those in the same age bracket, those from the same background. Is that a bad thing? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be handled fairly. Chapter 10 says openly, "everyone after his language, after their families, in their nations", so people gathering according to their own language and culture is in itself the normal state of things as God made it, and there is no need to feel guilty about it. To worship in your mother tongue, to pray in the accent of your home town — that is beautiful. The trouble comes at the next step: when that circle begins to decide who is allowed in, whose opinion counts and who is "one of us", then God-made diversity has turned into a man-made wall. The way to tell the difference is simple. Is your circle a home, or is it a door? A home adds another chair; a door only checks who you are.

The second question: our elders care a great deal about the clan register and the ancestral line, and some of them take real pride in their forebears — has that anything to do with chapter 10? My answer is that it has a great deal to do with it, and that it can be a bridge for the gospel. The impulse behind a Chinese family compiling its genealogy and the impulse behind Genesis writing genealogies have one thing in common: both of them believe that a human being does not simply appear out of nowhere — a person has an origin, a root, an account to be given. Scripture agrees with that completely; the whole Bible is busy recording family lines. The difference is the direction. A Chinese genealogy looks backwards, remembering where I came from. A biblical genealogy looks forwards, pointing to the One who was going to come out of this line. So you might say this to an elder: you are right to care about roots, that is a good thing; and I later came across a family record older than ours, which traces all the way down to one man, and that man died for me.
Some of the older people in my family are very taken up with the superiority of "our own kind". What should I do?

Start by separating two things. Taking pride in your own family, your culture and your language is good — that is an identity God gave you. Using it to look down on other people is where the problem lies. So there is no need to demand that an elder repudiate his own roots; that will usually only set up a confrontation. In practice: first, affirm what he treasures — there really are things in our family's way of life worth passing on. Second, do not echo remarks that belittle other people, and do not argue it out on the spot either; a gentle sentence can turn the subject. Third, demonstrate it by what you do — how you treat the person who has been looked down on carries more weight than any argument you make. Changing the mindset of a whole family is the work of years. It does not happen over one meal.
7. Living 321 Out — Passing the Blessing On Down the Line
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Nimrod was a hunter; the Lord Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd." A hunter counts how much he has taken in; a shepherd counts how well the sheep are doing. Brothers and sisters, that contrast goes straight to the heart of every co-worker who leads people. My role model here is very concrete: with the people I lead, the first thing I ask is not "what has he got done for me?" but "has he grown?"

The Bible is my standard — this chapter hands us a standard for looking at the world: every family on earth comes from one blood, and every one of them is on God's register. So racial superiority of any kind, discrimination by region, describing some group of people as innately inferior — none of it squares with Scripture. This standard is needed especially in today's online world, because despising a whole group of people at once is the easiest sin there is to commit and the one you are least likely to be called to account for.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — put chapter 10 side by side with Acts 2. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down, and every man heard the disciples telling the mighty works of God in the dialect of his own home. And that list of peoples in Acts 2 reads like an echo of Genesis 10. Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit did not take the languages back. The Holy Spirit taught the gospel to speak every one of them.

Let Jesus be King — verse 8 says Nimrod "began to be a mighty one in the earth", and the beginning of his kingdom was Babel. The same capability can be used to build your own name or to build God's kingdom. To let Jesus be King is to re-label the influence in your hands as belonging to him. Your eloquence, your contacts, your professional skill, your resources — whose name are you going to build with them this week?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice that not one hero is celebrated in this chapter, and the one man who does get a close-up has a question mark set against him by a city name. The protagonist of this chapter is God: scattering, setting boundaries, and keeping that one line safe.

Establish God's system — the seventy nations are registered one by one, and then God chooses one man in order to bless them. Brothers and sisters, God's system has never been about shutting other people out. To establish God's system is to keep passing the blessing on down the line, not to fence it off for our own use. If the names on your prayer list are all your own kind, this chapter is asking you to open it out a little.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on being of one mind, on unity, on the Goal — and that is right. But chapter 10 reminds us that unity is not uniformity. The world God made has seventy nations, seventy languages, seventy cultures, and his plan is to bless all of them, not to turn all of them into the same thing. So be careful whenever we are pushing any structure forward: if our unity in practice requires every single person to pray in the same manner, to speak with the same vocabulary and to serve with the same temperament, then what we are chasing may not be God's unity at all. It may be Babel's uniformity.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same List
Brothers and sisters, the same list of seventy nations, falling into four different kinds of heart, is read four completely different ways.

The proud heart finishes the chapter thinking, "Just as well I am on the right branch." This heart very easily produces an invisible hierarchy inside a church — the long-standing member ranks above the newcomer, people out of a certain stream are purer, a certain gift is more spiritual. Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end this chapter writes down seventy nations on the level, with no ranking at all. And Acts 10:34 says, "Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism."

The fearful heart finishes the chapter thinking, "So many nations, such an enormous world — can God really keep up with it all?" This heart panics very easily when a whole era is shaking. To that heart I want to say: this chapter was written precisely for you. God registers them nation by nation, and not one name is missing. Even the names that scholarship today can no longer identify are names he still remembers. He can keep up.

The ashamed heart finishes the chapter thinking, "My family has nothing worth putting on show." You may come from ordinary stock; your family may have no story; there may not be a single name on the register you could be proud of. Brothers and sisters, look at this chapter: the people who really did have renown — Nimrod, for instance — are the ones the text sets a question mark against. And the branch God finally chose runs down to a man who was told to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house, a man who laid every part of his background down. Where you come from does not decide your place in God's plan.

The wounded heart finishes the chapter thinking, "I am the one who has always been treated as an outsider." Because of your accent, your education, your background — or because you are divorced, or single, or ill — you may have been filed away in your group as "the different one." Brothers and sisters, the answer this chapter gives you is perfectly clear: being different is not the problem; being different is how God made it. The ones who treat difference as a problem are people, not God. And Ephesians 2:19 says, "So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God."
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, read this chapter through once and say the seventy names out loud, slowly. As you say them, hold one thought: God remembers every one of these people. When you have finished, the question "can God keep up?" will feel different to you.

Second, pray for one nation for seven days. Pick a country or a people group you know nothing at all about, or even feel some resistance towards, and pray for it one minute a day. That is the first step in opening out your prayer list.

Third, find the person in your church who is least like you, and take him out for a meal — or simply sit down and listen to him for twenty minutes. You do not have to persuade him, and you do not have to be persuaded by him. Only listen.

Fourth, check whose name your influence is building. This week write down three things you are working hard at, and beside each one write down honestly: if this comes off, who is the one who gets lifted up?

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: there is a whole chapter in the Bible that is a list of seventy nations, and in that period every genealogy was written to prove that one's own family was nobler than everybody else's; the Bible instead writes them all down side by side and on the level, and says the whole human race came from one blood; so here is what I have learned — the differences between people are not a problem to be ironed out, they were built in from the start.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the differences between people are God's own making, and I will no longer treat being different as a problem.
I declare that every family on earth is on God's register, and that I will not think less of any group of people.
I declare that I will be a shepherd and not a hunter; what I look at is whether people are growing, not how much I have taken in.
I declare that God did not choose me so that I could fence the blessing off for my own use, but so that I would pass it on down the line.
This week I am supposed to "pray for someone who is different from us" — but I don't seem to have anyone like that around me.

You almost certainly do; we have simply filed him under "someone I don't know well" rather than "someone different from me." Three ways to find him. First, in your neighbourhood, your company or your school, is there anyone who speaks a different language, comes from somewhere else, or holds a different faith? Second, in your own social world, is there a group of people you frown at the moment they are mentioned? That is usually where your "different" is. Third, in your extended family, is there a relative who has long been pushed out to the margin? And once you have found him, do not open with the gospel. Do one very small thing first: remember his name, ask him one question about himself, and listen until he has finished. Chapter 10 left a name for every single nation, and that in itself is the attitude we are meant to learn.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be a list and a man.

Chapter 10 is seventy nations, page after page of names, a whole world map spread out flat. At the end of chapter 11 the camera closes in and in until it rests on an old man who has no son. And in chapter 12 God says to him, "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you."

Brothers and sisters, do you see the arc? Seventy nations — one man — all the families of the earth. God narrowed from the whole world down onto one man, so that from that one man he could go back out to the whole world.

And the far end of that line is Revelation 7:9: "After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb."

Brothers and sisters — every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages: those are the four words of Genesis 10. That list of seventy nations is, at the end, standing before the throne, all of it. And they have not turned into one nation speaking one language. They are still every nation and all tribes and peoples and languages. They are simply singing the same song.
So this chapter is not a stretch of data you may skip. It is the root of mission, and it is the trailer for heaven.

The focus is not on which branch I belong to, not on whether my background is good enough, and not on who in the church happens to get on with me. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lamb who laid down his life for every nation and all tribes and peoples and languages. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to open our prayer lists out a little wider, and to give the person least like us twenty more minutes of listening. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Chapter 10 gathers every nation of the then-known world into one list, and all of them share a single origin. Where does that leave "racial superiority"?
2. ★★ This chapter is a funnel: from seventy nations down to one man. Why does God choose to work that way?
3. ★ The only man in the chapter with a story is Nimrod, and the beginning of his kingdom was Babel. What is the text hinting at by arranging it that way?
4. ★★ Whichever way you interpret the phrase "before Yahweh", it reminds us of one thing. What is that one thing?

Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it out, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (our group is the better one), fearful (those people will affect us), ashamed (I am the one who gets looked down on), wounded (I was once shut out because of where I came from). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a group of people you frown at the moment they are mentioned? You do not have to say who they are. Only say this: when did that aversion begin?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The measuring stick I use most often, to divide people into us and them, is …"
9. ★★ This week, what one small thing will you do for someone who is "not like you"? Say the time, the place and the person.

Leader's reminder: question seven may stir up political or ethnic loyalties. The leader must hold the line: no comment on political parties, no comment on countries, no naming of any group — deal only with the measuring stick inside each person's own heart. If the discussion starts turning into a debate, stop at once and go back to the text.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your extended family, is there a relative who has long been pushed out to the margin? What will you do for him this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who is most often treated as the outsider?

12. ★★★ The remembering-names practice: this week, learn the names of three people whose names you would not normally trouble to learn, and say them out loud to their faces. Say which three you will start with.
